questions.question: Define genocide and describe the stages by which Nazi persecution of Jews became genocide between 1939 and 1942.
questions.expected_answer: Genocide is the deliberate killing of members of a national, ethnic, racial or religious group with intent to destroy it in whole or part. After 1939 Polish Jews were forced into ghettos such as Warsaw, where starvation and disease killed many; Jews were marked with the yellow star. From June 1941 Einsatzgruppen shot Jewish communities in the Soviet Union (Babi Yar, September 1941). Gassing began at Chełmno in December 1941, and the Wannsee Conference of 20 January 1942 coordinated the Final Solution across Europe, leading to deportations to extermination camps.

questions.question: Distinguish between concentration camps and extermination camps and describe what happened to deportees at Auschwitz-Birkenau.
questions.expected_answer: Concentration camps (such as Dachau) imprisoned people in brutal forced labour; extermination camps (Chełmno, Bełżec, Sobibór, Treblinka, Majdanek, Auschwitz-Birkenau, all in occupied Poland) were built to murder on arrival. At Auschwitz, deportees arrived in sealed goods wagons; SS doctors made a selection on the ramp; a minority were tattooed and used as slave labour; most, including the old, sick, mothers and children, were murdered in gas chambers with Zyklon B and their bodies burned; belongings were seized. About 1,1 million people were murdered there.

questions.question: Explain the roles of perpetrators, bystanders and rescuers in the Holocaust, giving an example of a rescuer, and explain why the Holocaust is remembered today.
questions.expected_answer: Perpetrators planned and carried out the killing (SS, police, officials, collaborators). Bystanders saw and did nothing out of fear, indifference or self-interest, allowing it to continue. Rescuers risked their lives to save Jews, for example Irena Sendler (about 2 500 children), Oskar Schindler (about 1 200 workers) or the Danish rescue of about 7 000 Jews. It is remembered to honour the victims, to understand how hatred grows from words and laws to murder, to counter denial with evidence and to protect human rights.
